items.stem: A task is a single, well-specified transformation (reformat this text) with no external lookups. Why is a looping agent usually the wrong choice here?

options.text: A single model call is cheaper, faster and more predictable; a loop adds cost and failure modes with no benefit
options.rationale: Correct: agency pays off only when the task needs iteration, tools or branching that a single call cannot do.
They can; the point is a loop is unnecessary overhead for a one-shot transformation.

options.text: Single calls cannot use a system prompt
options.rationale: They can; this is irrelevant to the choice.
A loop adds variance and cost; it is not inherently more accurate.

items.stem: Which TWO are essential stopping conditions for an agent control loop? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A maximum number of steps or iterations
options.rationale: Correct: a step budget prevents an unbounded loop.

options.text: An explicit success or goal-reached check
options.rationale: Correct: the loop must recognise when the task is done.

options.text: A requirement that the model use every available tool
options.rationale: Forcing tool use is not a stopping condition and harms efficiency.

options.text: A rule that the agent must always run at least ten steps
options.rationale: A minimum-steps rule delays completion; it is not a stopping condition.

items.explanation: Correct: a step budget prevents an unbounded loop.

items.stem: An agent keeps re-running the same failing search and never finishes. What control-loop fix most directly addresses this?

options.text: Detect repeated identical actions and either replan or halt with an error after a bounded retry count
options.rationale: Correct: loop guards on repeated actions plus a retry bound break the cycle.
More randomness does not fix a missing loop guard and hurts reliability.
That makes the runaway loop worse.
More tools do not stop a repeated-action loop.

items.explanation: Correct: loop guards on repeated actions plus a retry bound break the cycle.
